paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Few episodes in economic history are retold as often as the Dutch tulip mania of the 1630s. In the familiar version, ordinary citizens of the Netherlands became so obsessed with tulip bulbs that they exchanged houses, land and life savings for a single flower, until prices collapsed in February 1637, leaving thousands ruined and the national economy in disarray. The story has become a standard warning in discussions of speculation, invoked whenever share prices or new kinds of asset seem to rise beyond reason. Yet the more closely historians have examined the surviving evidence, the less the familiar version seems to hold up, and I would argue that its enduring popularity tells us more about later generations than about the Dutch Republic itself.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Some elements of the story are not in dispute. Tulips, introduced to western Europe from the Ottoman Empire in the sixteenth century, had become luxury goods by the early seventeenth, prized by wealthy collectors for their intense colours. The most admired varieties displayed dramatic streaks and feathered patterns, which we now know were caused by a virus spread by aphids. Because the infection weakened the plants, these 'broken' tulips multiplied slowly, and their scarcity kept prices high. It is also clear that during the winter of 1636–37 prices for some bulbs rose extraordinarily fast before falling abruptly, and that trading effectively ceased within a matter of days.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Much of what is widely believed beyond this, however, rests on shaky foundations. The most influential account was written not by a contemporary but by the Scottish journalist Charles Mackay, whose popular book on 'extraordinary popular delusions' appeared in 1841, two centuries after the event. Mackay drew heavily on moralising pamphlets published in 1637, which were written to condemn speculation rather than to record it accurately. Stories that have been repeated ever since, such as that of a sailor who mistook a costly bulb for an onion and ate it with his herring, derive from these sources and cannot be verified. It is regrettable that such anecdotes have so often been presented as fact in textbooks.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The most thorough modern study, by the historian Anne Goldgar, examined notarial records, court documents and private papers from the period. She found no convincing evidence of widespread financial ruin: not a single documented bankruptcy that could be directly attributed to the tulip trade, and none of the suicides that later writers described. Those involved were mostly prosperous merchants and skilled craftsmen rather than the chimney sweeps and labourers of popular legend, and most could absorb their losses. What the collapse damaged, Goldgar argued, was less people's wealth than their confidence in shared judgements of value and in the honour of their trading partners.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The nature of the trade also helps to explain why the damage was limited. Bulbs remain underground for much of the year, so from the autumn onwards buyers typically signed contracts to purchase bulbs at a fixed price when they were lifted the following summer. Much of the frantic dealing of that winter took place in taverns, where such agreements were made with little or no money changing hands. When prices fell, many buyers simply refused to honour their contracts, and courts proved unwilling to enforce what they regarded as gambling debts. Eventually, local authorities allowed buyers to cancel agreements by paying a small fraction of the original price. In economic terms, therefore, much of the wealth that appeared to vanish had never really existed.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Some economists have gone further and questioned whether the episode was irrational at all. Peter Garber has pointed out that sharp falls in the price of rare bulbs were normal once a variety became more widely available, and that similar patterns can still be observed in the modern flower trade. Others have suggested that an outbreak of plague in Haarlem at the time may have made traders more willing to take risks. Such explanations are plausible, though in my view none fully accounts for the speed of the price rise in the final weeks, which does suggest that expectations of further gains had, for a brief period, become detached from any realistic assessment of value.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Why, then, has the exaggerated version survived? Part of the answer lies in its usefulness. A vivid tale of folly is more memorable than a careful account of futures contracts and municipal regulations, and commentators seeking to warn against a new financial fashion naturally reach for the most dramatic precedent available. The tulip story is also conveniently distant: it allows modern readers to observe irrational behaviour without recognising it in themselves. None of this means that speculative bubbles are imaginary; later crises have caused real and widespread hardship. But if the tulip episode is to serve as a lesson, it should perhaps be one about how easily a good story can triumph over the evidence.
